motion: Is belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God rational given alleged gratuitous evil, salvation confusion, rationality, design, and morality?

routes.description: Establish that belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational because the available evidence includes apparently gratuitous evil and confused salvation requirements, while the proposed arguments from reason, design, and morality do not adequately support that God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the conflict between the claimed divine attributes and the observed world, together with epistemic and salvation confusion, defeats or outweighs the cumulative positive case for rational theism.

bridges.description: Given the available reason and evidence, belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational.

Apparently gratuitous evil and related epistemic confusion outweigh the proposed arguments for God and prevent those arguments from rationally supporting the all-powerful, all-loving God under discussion.
Pervasive suffering that appears to serve no greater good is improbable under an all-powerful, all-loving God, and merely possible theodicies do not make belief in that God rational.
An all-loving God would not attach grave eternal consequences to salvation conditions that sincere people cannot reliably identify and religious communities cannot agree upon.

Evolutionary accounts of cognition and morality, together with alternative explanations of apparent design, undercut the claim that reason, fine-tuning, or moral experience rationally identifies the proposed God.

routes.description: Establish that belief in God is rational through a cumulative case from the reliability of reason, the life-permitting structure of the universe, and objective morality, while answering the evidential challenge from suffering.
routes.successCriteria: Show that rationality, design, and morality are collectively more expected or intelligible if God exists than if God does not, and that suffering does not defeat this cumulative support.

bridges.description: The cumulative available evidence makes belief in God more rational than nonbelief.

The combined evidence from rational minds, cosmic design, and objective morality makes God more probable than God's nonexistence, while available responses prevent suffering from defeating that inference.
Unguided naturalism undermines confidence that evolved minds track truth, whereas an intelligent creator provides a rational basis for trusting human reason and the universe's intelligibility.
The universe's highly specific life-permitting conditions are substantially more probable under intelligent design than under an unguided chance hypothesis.
Objective moral obligations are difficult to ground in an impersonal, purposeless universe but are intelligible when goodness is grounded in God.

sections.title: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
sections.rationale: Beginning with the debate’s definition of rational belief, this section groups the competing accounts of why human cognition can be trusted and the ensuing exchange over evolutionary truth-tracking and theistic reliability.

sections.title: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
sections.rationale: This section collects the initial evidential challenge from apparently purposeless suffering, the evil-God comparison, the concession about its significance, and the principal theistic accounts of normativity, afterlife, theodicy, and divine participation in suffering.

sections.title: Salvation Confusion and the Identity of God
sections.rationale: This section connects the critique of disputed salvation conditions with the cumulative case for rational theism and the later contention that generic creator arguments do not by themselves identify an all-powerful, all-loving religious God.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning and Evolutionary Accounts of Design
sections.rationale: This section places the cosmic fine-tuning argument alongside the later evolutionary account of apparent biological design, preserving the debate’s distinct but related explanations of ordered and life-permitting features.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: This section groups the moral argument for God, the evolutionary account of moral intuitions, and the extended exchange over whether goodness is independent of God, arbitrarily commanded, or grounded in the divine nature.
